description.narrative: Förändring och påverkan av globala marknader för stora handelsvaror (bomull, palmolja, tonfisk, timmer, papper/pappersmassa) i riktning mot mer hållbarhet.
Transforming global markets for commodities (cotton, palm oil, tuna, timber, pulp&paper) towards increased sustainability.

General question: Results related to the intended outcome 2014Question: Summarise results related to the intended outcome (this information will be sent to Open Aid)Answer: In a complex and difficult field, WWF has managed to launch and promote a number of certifications for various commodities and to secure commitments to sustainable sourcing from a large number of multilateral corporations. The program in this first phase showed results in more certified timber (8.4% to 14.9%); palm oil (6.3% to 16.3%); and tuna (0.5% to 12.9%) to mention a few. WWF Sweden was also part in the elaboration and launching of three completely new certification systems (farmed fish, sugar and beef) and has been very active in promoting the recently launched certification systems for palm oil, cotton and soybeans. Cooperation with and capacity building within the private sector, universities, financial institutions and authorities have been important results from the first phase which WWF Sweden will continue to build on in the second phase. An independant evaluation of the program concludes that the project has contributed to a shift in the market for some commodities. However, certification schemes for other commodities are still in their early stages and far from the overall MTI (Market Transformation Initiative) target of 25% certified production by 2020. This is especially evident in emerging economies and with companies based in these economies.
It is more difficult to assess whether the intervention had long term development impacts. This is partly due to the lack of a robust results framework, but has also to do with the evidence base with regards to certification and poverty reduction effects. A study by International Institute for Sustainable Development (iisd) concluded that "voluntary sustainability standards offer an important contribution to the green economy but cannot be assumed to deliver sustainable development outcomes." These issues have been addressed in the design of phase two of the intervention with increased explicit emphasis on poverty reduction and a more thorough results framework and an updated theory of change. There is a wide variety of standards available, and Sida's assessment is that the WWF supported standards are far more wide reaching than others in terms of stakeholder influence and transparency. By supporting the growth and constant improvement of these standards, Sida will also contribute to the reduction of weaker standards.
